answer.observations: The baseline shows UDP taking essentially the whole 1Gbps link while TCP delivers 0 bps and the reverse link carries 0 bps; this suggests TCP may not be getting ACKs at all, not merely losing bandwidth to UDP.

whys.result: tcp_goodput_bps=0, l1_util_back=0.0, and tcp_retrans=3 in the default run.
whys.guess: TCP never establishes a usable connection; UDP fills the sender-side queue before TCP can get handshake or data packets through, so no ACKs return.

whys.result: l1_util=0.999999, udp_loss_frac=0.510489, and l1_drops=911591 with UDP offered at 2Gbps on a 1Gbps link.
whys.guess: The FIFO queue is persistently full because UDP alone offers twice the link rate, so any TCP packet arriving when the queue is full is tail-dropped.

whys.result: tcp_retrans=3 over the measured interval while tcp_goodput_bps=0.
whys.guess: The retransmission count is consistent with a few initial-RTO SYN retransmissions rather than data-segment losses after a connection is established.

answer.observations: The series shows tcp_cwnd briefly at 14480 (10 MSS) at t=1.1 then dropping to 1448 (1 MSS) and staying there, yet tcp_bps=0 throughout. This means the TCP handshake completed but every data segment was lost. The reverse link carries 0 bps, so ACKs never returned — the receiver never got a complete TCP segment to acknowledge.

whys.result: tcp_cwnd=14480 at t=1.1 then 1448 from t=2.1 onward, tcp_bps=0, tcp_retrans=3, l1_util_back=0.0: the handshake completed (cwnd set to 10 MSS) but every data segment was lost and no ACK returned.
whys.guess: The forward FIFO queue is permanently full because UDP alone offers 2× the link rate, so TCP data segments (even a single MSS after timeout) are tail-dropped before reaching the receiver; no ACKs are generated, so the reverse link carries nothing.

whys.result: l1_q stays at 99-100 for the entire measured window with queue=100, confirming the queue is persistently full; tcp_cwnd stuck at 1 MSS (1448 bytes) means TCP backed off to minimum after repeated losses.
whys.guess: Because the queue is always full, the problem is structural (FIFO tail-drop with no fairness), not a congestion-control problem: no TCP variant can get data through a permanently-full FIFO queue regardless of its loss/delay response.

hypotheses.text: With queue=100, TcpBbr will also show tcp_goodput_bps ≈ 0 because the FIFO queue is always full and BBR's loss-tolerance cannot overcome tail-drop of every segment.
Increasing queue to 1000 will not give TCP nonzero goodput because TCP segments will still be tail-dropped once the larger queue fills; tcp_goodput_bps remains ≈ 0.
With queue=4, the queue drains fast enough between UDP arrivals to occasionally admit a TCP segment, so tcp_goodput_bps > 0 (unlike queue=100).

answer.observations: The probe readings show tcp_inflight max 14480 and tcp_rtt_ms max 1.0, but these may be initial socket state; I need RTO, ssthresh, rwnd, and reverse device queue to tell whether TCP ever got ACKs or only retransmits SYNs.

The probe shows TCP in repeated RTO backoff with zero reverse traffic, but it does not yet show whether TCP is blocked at handshake/initial admission or merely losing established data. I need to see whether a larger queue or a scheduler admits TCP and produces ACKs.

whys.result: In r001, tcp_rto_ms goes 1000->2000->4000->8000, tcp_ssthresh min is 2896, tcp_rwnd min is 65535, l1_devq_back max is 0, and tcp_bps is 0.
whys.guess: TCP receives no ACKs during the measured interval; it is stuck in RTO retransmissions/restarts, so zero goodput is an admission or handshake failure at the full sender queue.

whys.result: In r001, l1_q stays 99-100 and l1_wait_ms p95 is 1.144 ms while UDP offers 2 Gbps on a 1 Gbps link.
whys.guess: The FIFO is saturated; TCP can enter only during the initial fill window or when a service event creates space, so queue length controls whether its first packets are admitted.

whys.result: In r001, tcp_cwnd falls to 1448 bytes and tcp_ssthresh to 2896 bytes while tcp_bps is 0.
whys.guess: Cubic's loss response collapses its window under UDP-caused loss; a loss-tolerant controller like BBR may retain more sending rate once TCP is admitted.

hypotheses.text: With TcpCubic, a 1000-packet queue admits TCP's initial packets, producing reverse ACK traffic and tcp_goodput_bps above 10 kbps, while a 4-packet queue does not beat it.
Replacing the sender FIFO with a scheduler that gives each flow a link share makes tcp_goodput_bps positive and larger than the FIFO q1000 run, because TCP no longer competes for tail-drop spaces.
With l1.queue.length=1000, TcpBbr delivers more tcp_goodput_bps than TcpCubic because UDP-induced losses do not force BBR to collapse its window.

decision_rules.decision_rule: tcp_goodput_bps@q1000_cubic > 10000 AND l1_util_back@q1000_cubic > 0.0001 AND tcp_goodput_bps@q1000_cubic > tcp_goodput_bps@q4_cubic * 1.01

answer.observations: H1 predicts that a 1000-packet queue admits TCP's first packets and creates reverse ACK traffic, while a 4-packet queue does not beat it; the current records only show the 100-packet default fails.

decision_rules.decision_rule: tcp_goodput_bps@q1000_cubic > 10000 AND l1_util_back@q1000_cubic > 0 AND tcp_goodput_bps@q4_cubic <= tcp_goodput_bps@q1000_cubic * 1.01

answer.observations: The current records show zero measured reverse traffic for the default run, but they do not show whether a larger queue can admit TCP enough to create ACKs during the measured interval; this is the first gate for any TCP goodput.

hypotheses.text: With TcpCubic, a 1000-packet queue admits TCP during the measured interval and produces reverse ACK traffic (l1_util_back > 0), whereas a 4-packet queue does not (l1_util_back = 0).

drop.why: H1 mixed queue admission with Cubic's loss response; G8 showed its rule could pass under the admission-only rival, so it is dropped in favor of a direct admission test.

answer.observations: The probe shows a persistently full sender queue and no reverse traffic, but it does not show whether TCP is blocked only by admission or also by RTO backoff; this matters for whether queue length or a service-guaranteeing queue can help.

drop.why: G9 showed the queue-length admission rule could pass under a service/admission rival, so it does not test the intended cause; I will replace it with a service-guarantee test.

answer.observations: T12-T17 show TCP in RTO backoff with inflight fixed at 1448 bytes and the sender queue never below 99 packets, but they do not show whether TCP type matters before admission or whether a scheduler can break the trap.

whys.result: In r001, tcp_rto_ms first exceeds 3999 at 4.1 s and 7999 at 8.1 s while tcp_inflight min is 1448 bytes, tcp_cwnd min is 1448 bytes, and l1_q min is 99 packets.
whys.guess: TCP is stuck in an RTO/admission trap: its initial or retransmitted packets are dropped by the full FIFO before ACKs can clock it, so congestion-control type cannot matter until admission is changed.

whys.result: The same run shows no reverse traffic while RTO doubles, so the measured interval never reaches a loss-controlled steady state.
whys.guess: A scheduler that gives TCP a service share should create ACKs and positive TCP goodput even at a tiny queue, whereas FIFO q4 should keep both Cubic and BBR starved.

hypotheses.text: With FIFO q4, TcpCubic and TcpBbr are both starved before ACK clocking: tcp_goodput_bps is below 1 Mbps and l1_util_back is below 0.001 for both.
With TcpCubic and q4, replacing the sender FIFO with a scheduler produces reverse ACK traffic and TCP goodput above 100 Mbps, while FIFO q4 does not.

decision_rules.decision_rule: tcp_goodput_bps@fifo_q4_cubic < 1000000 AND l1_util_back@fifo_q4_cubic < 0.001 AND tcp_goodput_bps@fifo_q4_bbr < 1000000 AND l1_util_back@fifo_q4_bbr < 0.001
